kaigo-atomic-heart-diseases.heading: Blocked or bleeding brain vessels and heart function
paragraphs: An ischemic stroke occurs when a brain vessel is blocked and blood cannot reach an area. This differs from cerebral hemorrhage and other bleeding caused by a ruptured vessel. Effects depend on injury location and extent. Do not decide abilities from the disease name alone.

Angina relates to temporarily insufficient blood flow to heart muscle, for example from narrowed coronary arteries. In myocardial infarction, blocked coronary flow or similar problems damage heart muscle and cause necrosis, meaning cell or tissue death. A care worker cannot distinguish these diagnoses from descriptions such as very painful or mildly painful alone. Hypertension, diabetes and coronary changes may contribute to heart disease; confirm personal diagnosis and treatment information with healthcare professionals.

In heart failure, reduced heart function and difficulty supplying enough blood for bodily needs can cause various symptoms. Breathlessness, palpitations, fatigue, swelling, weight gain and urine changes provide observation clues. One alone does not establish heart failure.

Cerebrovascular disease may involve headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting or changes in consciousness, sensation or breathing, but these are not exclusive symptoms. Do not delay urgent help and calls for sudden limb paralysis, speech changes, sudden breathlessness or severe chest pain. Seek help without waiting to establish the cause.

Do not impose a posture seen in an example on someone with breathlessness. Forward-leaning sitting is an explanatory example, not an instruction for everyone. Report condition and distress and support a tolerable posture according to healthcare instructions and the individual care plan. Arranging posture does not establish recovery.

Salt, fluids and activity adjustments follow treatment and care plans based on individual assessment. Hearing ‘heart failure’ does not authorize workers to reduce drinking or insist on continued exercise. Distinguish long-term food and activity management from initial action for sudden changes.

This explanation teaches how diseases arise and the boundaries of observation and reporting. Tell healthcare professionals when you made the observation, what the person said, how the situation differs from usual and what action you took. This material does not provide instructions for diagnosis or changes to treatment.

[Learning example] Hearing a heart-failure diagnosis, a worker reduces drinking and tries to continue activity without checking the person’s plan. Consider current condition and necessary contact instead of inventing instructions from a disease name.

kaigo-atomic-pneumonia.heading: Distinguish dysphagia, aspiration and pneumonia
paragraphs: Pneumonia is lung inflammation involving factors such as bacteria or viruses. Fever, fatigue, poor appetite, cough and sputum may occur. Older people may lack a clear collection of typical symptoms, so consider differences from usual too.

Dysphagia means difficulty in the swallowing process. Aspiration means material intended for the esophagus enters the airway. These related terms are not identical; not every swallowing difficulty is aspiration.

Besides food and drink, saliva containing bacteria can enter the airway and contribute to aspiration pneumonia. No observed coughing during a meal does not guarantee no aspiration, because aspiration can occur without an obvious cough.

Oral cleanliness and suitable eating posture and texture matter for managing risk. However, one measure cannot prevent all aspiration or pneumonia. Check swallowing condition and assessment needs with responsible professionals such as nurses or speech-language therapists.

Avoiding lying down immediately after meals also follows condition and plan. With breathlessness, coughing or changes in voice, expression or other concerns, stop feeding and arrange help and reporting through facility methods rather than continuing to test it. Do not independently change fluids, posture or texture.
This teaches observation and reporting, not independent diagnosis, swallowing tests, medication or improvised emergency techniques.
[Learning example] No obvious cough occurs during eating. Consider whether that alone establishes absence of aspiration.

kaigo-atomic-diabetes-types.heading: Differences between type 1 and type 2 diabetes
paragraphs: Diabetes involves persistently high blood glucose. Insulin helps body cells use glucose from the blood. In type 1, mainly immune-related damage to insulin-producing pancreatic cells causes insulin deficiency.

Type 1 is more common in children and younger people but can develop at any age. Older age does not establish type 2. Workers refer to a healthcare-confirmed diagnosis rather than deciding type from symptoms or age.
Type 2 involves reduced insulin effectiveness and insufficient secretion for needs. Multiple factors, including lifestyle, contribute. Do not reduce it to overeating alone or blame the person.

Thirst, increased drinking, increased urine, fatigue and unexplained weight loss can occur with high glucose, but symptoms may also be few. Report observed changes. Glucose measurement and treatment follow the agreed plan and assigned scope.
This lesson introduces types and observations. It does not authorize care workers to independently decide meal amounts, activity or medication doses and types.
[Learning example] A worker assumes an older person’s diabetes must be type 2. Consider the evidence needed to establish the type.

kaigo-atomic-diabetes-complications.heading: Diabetic complications and skin observation
paragraphs: Diabetes may cause retinal, kidney and peripheral-nerve complications. Eyes, kidneys and nerves are different sites, not one identical symptom. Coordinate prevention and management with healthcare professionals.

If nerve damage reduces sensation, a person may feel little pain even when they have a wound. Persistent high blood glucose may also make wounds slower to heal. The person’s statement that they do not feel pain is important information, but it is separate from evidence that there is no wound or that the situation is safe.

If you find a wound, redness, skin breakdown or a similar change, report its location, observed appearance, the person’s sensation and the time you noticed it according to the facility’s plan. Do not omit the record because there is no pain, or independently apply medication and obscure how the condition develops.

Meals, activity and medication are combined in the person’s treatment plan. Listen to satisfaction and wishes while avoiding independent restrictions or medication changes. Consult the person responsible about difficulties.
This teaches observation and coordination, not wound diagnosis or treatment methods.
[Learning example] A skin wound is present, but the person reports no pain. Record the statement separately from skin condition.

kaigo-atomic-visual-patterns.heading: Visual acuity, fields and spatial attention
paragraphs: Reduced vision may be congenital or arise from illness, accident or aging. Visual acuity concerns distinguishing detail; visual field concerns the area visible while looking. Some people see nothing, some detect light and some see a limited area. Vision differs individually.

With a central scotoma, the center of what the person looks toward may be unclear while surroundings remain visible. A narrowed field limits the visible area. Larger text may help but does not restore a lost visual field.

Unilateral spatial neglect involves difficulty attending to one side of space or objects because of brain dysfunction. It differs from loss of one side of the visual field, although both can coexist. Vision and spatial awareness require separate assessment.

One missed side of a tray does not establish cause or support needs. Ask how the person sees and check object positions, lighting, print and explanations against assessment and wishes. Do not move items without permission and remove orientation clues.
This teaches differences in vision. Do not equate black diagram areas with a person’s actual field or let workers diagnose disease or impairment location.
[Learning example] The person overlooks one side of a tray. Consider whether larger text alone is sufficient and what needs checking.

kaigo-atomic-internal-disability.heading: Protect devices and excretion routes with internal-organ impairments
paragraphs: Some people with heart-function or rhythm problems use pacemakers. Follow confirmed instructions for the person’s device, such as avoiding strong impacts to its implant site. Device use alone does not justify banning every activity or changing settings.

People with substantially reduced kidney function may receive dialysis. Hemodialysis sends blood through an external machine to remove some waste and excess water before returning it. Protecting the vascular access route matters.

Check the treatment team’s individual instructions for load on the access arm, bathing days and methods, and salt and fluid amounts. A learning-table example does not justify banning bathing for everyone on dialysis days or imposing identical fluid reductions. Promptly report bleeding, swelling and other noticed abnormalities through agreed methods.

Portable oxygen cylinders and concentrators used in oxygen therapy differ from ventilators supporting ventilation. Oxygen supports combustion, so contact with flames can cause fires or severe burns. Do not independently change prescribed flow or device settings.

For life with oxygen, check fire avoidance, infection prevention and preparation for power or supply interruption through device instructions and facility or home-support plans. Backup power or supply requirements depend on the device used.

Depending on disease or surgery, some people pass stool or urine through an abdominal opening called a stoma. Stool and urinary stomas differ in location and mechanism. Not everyone with bladder dysfunction has a stoma.

Handle stoma appliances and excreted material according to the person’s plan and the necessary training. Report redness or skin breakdown around the stoma, leaks and changes from usual. A worker without the relevant experience must not improvise adjustments to the appliance or opening.
This teaches equipment distinctions and support boundaries. Do not perform dialysis, oxygen, pacemaker or stoma operations or procedures from this text alone.
[Learning example] A worker applies a learning-table example about dialysis-day bathing to everyone. Separate individual instructions from general knowledge.

kaigo-atomic-mental-health.heading: Distinguish intellectual disability from mental-health difficulties
paragraphs: Intellectual disability relates to difficulties in intellectual functioning and adaptation arising during development. Understand it separately from difficulties related to mental illness. Support varies even under the same label, so check personal understanding and daily-life difficulties.
Do not treat adults as children because understanding takes time. Offer explanations and choices suited to life history, current life stage and wishes. Notice abilities as well as difficulties.

Mental illnesses include different conditions such as schizophrenia and mood disorders. Some people have difficulty regulating judgment or actions during stronger symptoms, but a diagnosis does not establish permanent incapacity or dangerousness. Check current condition and the individual support plan.

Depression can involve low mood and reduced interest; mania can involve unusually elevated mood and increased activity. One meeting with few words or cheerful talkativeness does not establish a diagnosis. Specifically report differences from usual, timing and personal difficulties.

Hallucinations are perceptions without corresponding external stimuli. Delusions include strongly held beliefs despite conflict with reality. Hearing voices or sounds without corresponding sounds is an auditory hallucination, one type of hallucination. Assessment requires professionals. Acknowledging fear or distress differs from confirming the content as fact.

Do not argue the person into submission or stop listening because of a diagnosis. Calmly check difficulties and arrange needed support. For sudden conditions threatening safety, seek the facility’s emergency response. This is not a diagnostic or medication-adjustment guide.
[Learning example] The person is cheerful and talkative in one conversation. Consider whether that alone justifies recording mania.

85.title: Blocked or bleeding brain vessels and heart function
objectives: Explain differences between ischemic stroke, cerebral hemorrhage and heart diseases.
Distinguish urgent contact from management under an individual treatment plan.
85.context: [Learning example] Hearing a heart-failure diagnosis, a worker reduces drinking and tries to continue activity without checking the person’s plan. Consider current condition and necessary contact instead of inventing instructions from a disease name.
85.artCaption: Share noticed changes with the nurse. The image alone cannot diagnose cardiac or cerebrovascular disease.

86.title: Distinguish dysphagia, aspiration and pneumonia
objectives: Distinguish dysphagia, aspiration and aspiration pneumonia.
Do not guarantee safety from absence of coughing alone; observe and report.
86.context: [Learning example] No obvious cough occurs during eating. Consider whether that alone establishes absence of aspiration.
86.artCaption: Staff check meal information together. Communicate observations separately from the person’s own words.

87.title: Differences between type 1 and type 2 diabetes
objectives: Distinguish type 1 and type 2 mechanisms without deciding type from age alone.
Understand changes seen with high glucose and the boundary against independent treatment changes.
87.context: [Learning example] A worker assumes an older person’s diabetes must be type 2. Consider the evidence needed to establish the type.
87.artCaption: This scene concerns dietary-plan consultation. Meal photos and age do not establish diabetes type.

88.title: Diabetic complications and skin observation
objectives: Distinguish eye, kidney and nerve complications.
Observe and report pain statements separately from skin condition.
88.context: [Learning example] A skin wound is present, but the person reports no pain. Record the statement separately from skin condition.
88.artCaption: Check changes from usual and contact healthcare professionals. This image is not a diagnosed diabetic-complication result.

89.title: Visual acuity, fields and spatial attention
objectives: Explain differences between acuity, visual fields and spatial attention.
Do not determine cause or support from one missed item alone.
89.context: [Learning example] The person overlooks one side of a tray. Consider whether larger text alone is sufficient and what needs checking.
89.artCaption: Discuss explanations that make seeing and choosing easier. The image alone does not determine visual fields or impairment location.

90.title: Protect devices and excretion routes with internal-organ impairments
objectives: Check individual instructions, training and abnormality-reporting requirements.
90.context: [Learning example] A worker applies a learning-table example about dialysis-day bathing to everyone. Separate individual instructions from general knowledge.
90.artCaption: Staff check an individual support plan. This does not illustrate pacemaker, dialysis or oxygen-device operation.

91.title: Distinguish intellectual disability from mental-health difficulties
objectives: Respect adult dignity without confusing intellectual disability and mental illness.
Report specific changes rather than diagnosing from mood or conversation quantity alone.
91.context: [Learning example] The person is cheerful and talkative in one conversation. Consider whether that alone justifies recording mania.
91.artCaption: Listen respectfully to concerns. Expression or one conversation alone does not establish a mental-illness diagnosis.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-heart-diseases.prompt: A worker reduces fluids and insists on continued activity based only on the label heart failure. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Do not set fluids or activity from the label alone; check current changes and the individual plan and seek help for sudden abnormalities.
Reduce everyone to the same intake without asking about swelling.
Finish planned exercise before contact despite breathlessness.
Rule out myocardial infarction because chest pain is mild.
rationales: A diagnosis does not establish that day’s limits. Separate initial urgent action from management after assessment.
This imposes uniform restrictions without checking condition and individual instructions.
Do not delay help or contact for sudden concerns such as breathlessness.
Pain severity alone cannot distinguish these diagnoses.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-pneumonia.prompt: No cough occurred during eating. Does that guarantee no aspiration?
options: No cough removes all future swallowing-assessment needs.
Change to regular food independently because there was no cough.
Oral care completely removes aspiration and pneumonia risks.
Aspiration can lack a cough; consider swallowing, observations and individual assessment and plan together.
rationales: Aspiration may lack an obvious cough, so this does not justify omitting assessment.
One observation does not authorize changing the plan.
Oral care matters but does not guarantee complete risk removal.
Do not judge by cough alone; arrange needed assessment and support.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-diabetes-types.prompt: Must an older person’s diabetes be type 2?
options: Record type 2 from age without checking diagnosis.
Refer to healthcare-confirmed diagnosis rather than age; type 1 can develop in adulthood too.
Diagnose type 2 from eating a large amount alone.
Both types have identical mechanisms and need no distinction.
rationales: Age alone cannot establish the type.
Type 1 is not limited to young people; do not replace diagnosis with assumptions.
Type 2 has several contributing factors and cannot be diagnosed from intake alone.
Distinguish mechanisms such as insulin deficiency and reduced effectiveness.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-diabetes-compli.prompt: A person with diabetes has a wound but reports no pain. What is appropriate?
options: Record and report observed injury separately from sensation; pain alone does not establish wound presence.
Omit wound records if painless.
No pain proves no nerve damage.
Apply medication independently without checking the plan or reporting.
rationales: Reduced sensation can make pain an incomplete indicator of wound condition.
The observed wound is separate information from pain.
No pain does not prove normal nerve function.
Independent treatment must not obstruct condition assessment or information sharing.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-visual-patterns.prompt: The person misses one side of a tray. Is larger text alone necessarily enough?
options: Every one-sided oversight is the same eye disease.
Enlarging print restores lost visual fields.
Check vision and spatial awareness and consider support matching assessment.
Clear everything without explanation after any one-sided oversight.
rationales: Different factors such as field loss and spatial attention need distinguishing.
Enlargement does not restore the visual field itself.
Do not decide cause from one behavior; distinguish acuity, field and attention.
Preserve choice and orientation clues while first checking condition and support methods.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-internal-disabi.prompt: Can a learning-table example for dialysis-day bathing be applied identically to everyone?
options: The table removes the need for individual instructions.
Protect vascular access and condition and check treatment-team instructions for bathing, salt and fluids.
Everyone receiving dialysis tolerates the same access-arm load.
Independently set fluid restrictions from the diagram.
rationales: General explanations are not personal treatment instructions.
Condition and treatment plan govern care; examples do not become universal instructions.
Access routes and personal conditions require individual checks.
A diagram cannot establish each person’s fluid needs.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-mental-health.prompt: The person is cheerful and talkative once. May this be recorded as mania?
options: Diagnose from word count alone.
Cheerful talk always establishes danger.
Mental concerns require no record of changes from usual.
Record specific speech and usual-pattern differences and leave diagnosis to professional assessment.
rationales: Conversation quantity alone lacks needed diagnostic information.
Do not assume danger from enjoyment or a diagnosis.
Specific changes help identify necessary support.
Communicate difficulties and changes without replacing one impression with a disease label.
